Some people don't have enough money even to buy enough food, and that's very unfair. People who are hungry don't have a choice. Hunger and lack of access are real problems, and people who are hungry have no choice. But veganism is addressed to those who can choose, and the person raising the objection almost always can. The basis of a vegan diet, rice, beans, potatoes and vegetables, is the most accessible food. And veganism isn't "a thing for rich white people": in India, about 39% of adults describe themselves as vegetarian, and there are meat-free traditions in many cultures.

text.bold: 1. It uses those without a choice to justify those with one.

paragraph.text: The same pattern as D7. Veganism already allows exceptions for those who can't.
Rice, beans, potatoes, oats and vegetables are among the cheapest and most available foods in most countries (J1).

text.bold: 3. Refusing meat isn't exclusive to rich white people.

paragraph.text: In India, about 39% of adults describe themselves as vegetarian, and 81% follow some restriction on eating meat. Vegetarianism isn't veganism, and India consumes a lot of milk; but the figure shows that not eating animals is far from being a habit of a white elite. There are vegetarian traditions in Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, Rastafarianism and many other cultures.

text.bold: 4. The argument usually comes from those who have a choice.

paragraph.text: That doesn't invalidate it, but it shows it speaks about other people: for whoever says it, the moral question still stands.

text.bold: 5. Hunger doesn't depend on veganism, but livestock doesn't help.

paragraph.text: Hunger is above all a problem of poverty and distribution, not a lack of food. Even so, livestock farming uses most farmland to produce a small fraction of calories (H9), and a more plant-based system could feed more people with the same land.

text.bold: 6. Exploiting animals is what is elitist.

paragraph.text: The charge of elitism holds for some lines of industrialized vegan products, which do cost more. But veganism is not aimed at specific groups: it is the refusal to exploit those who can suffer. Treating someone as usable because they have less power is exactly the logic of superiority we associate with elitism, and it is the logic that sustains animal exploitation.

(d) The strongest counter-reply: the vegan movement is sometimes elitist

The most serious version grants that veganism is possible for many, but criticizes how part of the movement presents itself: with expensive products, distant language and little attention to inequality.

text.bold: The criticism doesn't change the moral question.

paragraph.text: For those who can choose, the question remains.

Hunger and inequality are serious problems, and they deserve to be fought. But they don't justify those who can choose continuing to choose the option that requires animals' deaths. For those with a choice, the moral question still stands.

Unequal access to food is real and serious, and the vegan movement needs to pay attention to it, without judging those who have no choice and without presenting veganism as an expensive lifestyle. The criticism of elitism has substance.
But a vegan diet can be one of the most accessible, it exists in many cultures, and it's addressed to those who can choose. For them, other people's inequality isn't an excuse.
